notes:
1. Planning Commission — Background and Establishment

  • After Independence, India adopted planned economic development to address poverty, unemployment, low productivity, weak industrialisation and inadequate infrastructure.
  • Scarce financial and physical resources had to be directed towards national priorities.
  • The Planning Commission became the central institution for coordinating national development planning.
  • It was established on 15 March 1950 by a resolution of the Government of India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission → 15 March 1950

2. Planning Commission — Constitutional and Legal Status

  • It was created through an executive resolution of the Union Government.
  • It was not created by the Constitution.
  • It was not established by an Act of Parliament.
  • It was therefore both non-constitutional and non-statutory.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission → Executive Resolution + Non-Constitutional + Non-Statutory

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Planning Commission ≠ Constitutional Body

Planning Commission ≠ Statutory Body

3. Planning Commission — Main Development Role

  • It coordinated India's national development strategy for more than six decades.
  • It was closely associated with the Five-Year Plan system.
  • It helped convert broad development objectives into sectoral priorities, resource allocations and policy recommendations.

4. Planning Commission — Composition

The Commission broadly consisted of:

  • Chairman.
  • Deputy Chairman.
  • Full-time members.
  • Other members as determined by the Union Government.
  • The exact composition changed over time.

5. Prime Minister — Chairman

  • The Prime Minister of India served as the ex officio Chairman of the Planning Commission.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission Chairman → Prime Minister

6. Deputy Chairman — Role and Status

  • The Deputy Chairman was appointed by the Union Government.
  • The Deputy Chairman generally handled much of the day-to-day functioning.
  • The post generally enjoyed Cabinet Minister status.
📌 Must-Memorise

Deputy Chairman → Day-to-Day Leadership + Cabinet Minister Status

7. Full-Time Members and Expert Representation

  • Full-time members were generally specialists or experienced administrators.
  • Expertise could come from economics, administration, agriculture, industry, science, technology, finance and social development.
  • Union Ministers and other experts could also participate in planning-related discussions.

8. Planning Commission — Main Objectives

The Commission aimed to promote:

  • Economic growth.
  • Higher national income.
  • Higher living standards.
  • Employment.
  • Poverty reduction.
  • Agricultural development.
  • Industrial development.
  • Infrastructure expansion.
  • Balanced regional development.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Social justice.
  • Self-reliance.

9. Growth with Social Justice

  • The Planning Commission did not treat development as output growth alone.
  • It increasingly attempted to combine economic growth with social justice and wider human development.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning → Growth + Social Justice

10. Planning Commission — Resource Assessment

  • One of its major functions was to assess India's available resources.

These included:

  • Material resources.
  • Capital resources.
  • Human resources.
  • It also identified resource shortages and suggested measures to mobilise additional resources.

11. Planning Commission — Plan Formulation and Priority Setting

  • It formulated development plans for the effective and balanced use of resources.
  • It determined priorities among competing sectors and programmes.
  • Scarce resources were directed towards activities considered most important for national development.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission → Plan Formulation + Priority Setting

12. Planning Commission — Resource Allocation

  • The Commission recommended allocation of resources among development activities.
  • Resource allocation became one of its most influential functions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission → Resource Allocation

13. Planning Commission — Implementation Review and Policy Correction

  • It examined conditions necessary for successful Plan implementation.
  • It periodically reviewed the progress of Five-Year Plans and development programmes.
  • It recommended policy changes when implementation problems or changing economic conditions required correction.

14. Planning Commission — Advisory Role

  • It advised the Union Government and State Governments on economic and development-related matters.

15. Planning Commission — Core Planning Cycle

The broad planning cycle was:

Resource Assessment

→ Priority Setting

→ Plan Formulation

→ Resource Allocation

→ Implementation Review

→ Evaluation

📌 Must-Memorise

Assess → Prioritise → Plan → Allocate → Review → Evaluate

16. Planning Commission and Five-Year Plans

  • The Planning Commission was the principal institution responsible for preparing India's Five-Year Plans.
  • Five-Year Plans formed the core of national development strategy for several decades.
  • The Commission remained associated with planning from the First Plan beginning in 1951 through the Twelfth Plan period.

17. Five-Year Plan Preparation — Main Inputs

During Plan preparation, the Commission examined:

  • National economic conditions.
  • Development priorities.
  • Financial resources.
  • Sectoral requirements.
  • Long-term development needs.

18. Five-Year Plan Preparation — Consultation

The Commission consulted:

  • Union Ministries.
  • State Governments.
  • Experts.
  • Specialised institutions.
  • Sector-specific requirements and State development priorities were incorporated into the broader planning process.

19. Five-Year Plans — Major Sectoral Coverage

Plans commonly covered:

  • Agriculture.
  • Irrigation.
  • Industry.
  • Energy.
  • Transport.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Employment.
  • Rural development.
  • Social welfare.

20. Draft Plans and Finalisation

  • Draft Plans were prepared and discussed before final approval and implementation.
  • Planning therefore involved consultation, revision and coordination rather than a single administrative decision.

21. Planning Commission — Resource Estimation

Development resources were estimated from:

  • Government revenue.
  • Domestic savings.
  • Public borrowing.
  • Foreign assistance.
  • Institutional finance.
  • Physical resources.
  • Human resources.

22. Planning Commission — Matching Resources with Priorities

  • The Commission attempted to match available financial and physical resources with national development priorities.
  • This linked development ambitions with the actual resource capacity of the economy.

23. Plan and Non-Plan Expenditure — Historical Classification

  • Government expenditure was historically divided into Plan Expenditure and Non-Plan Expenditure.
  • Plan expenditure was associated with programmes included in the planning framework.
  • Non-Plan expenditure broadly covered recurring or committed expenditure outside that classification.
  • This distinction was later discontinued.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Plan / Non-Plan Expenditure → Historical Classification

Do not treat it as the present expenditure structure.

24. Planning Commission and State Development

  • State Governments were important participants because many development subjects fell within State jurisdiction.

Important State-level areas included:

  • Agriculture.
  • Irrigation.
  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Rural development.
  • State roads.
  • Local infrastructure.

25. State Plan Discussions

  • State Governments presented development priorities and financial requirements to the Planning Commission.
  • These discussions became an important feature of Centre-State planning relations.

26. Planning Commission — Review of State Plans

  • The Commission reviewed State Plans in relation to national priorities and available resources.
  • Its resource-allocation role gave it considerable influence over State development programmes.

27. Centre-State Planning Relationship

  • National planning combined Union priorities with State development needs.
  • The Planning Commission acted as an important coordinating institution between the two levels.

28. National Development Council — 1952

  • The National Development Council, or NDC, was established in 1952.
  • It was created to strengthen cooperation among the Union Government, State Governments and the Planning Commission.
📌 Must-Memorise

National Development Council → 1952

29. NDC — Composition and Leadership

  • The Prime Minister served as Chairman of the NDC.
  • Chief Ministers of States participated.
  • Union Ministers and other representatives also took part.
📌 Must-Memorise

NDC Chairman → Prime Minister

States → Chief Ministers

30. NDC — Main Role

The NDC:

  • Considered major national Plans.
  • Discussed development policies.
  • Provided a forum for Union-State consultation.
  • Brought State perspectives into national planning.

31. Planning Commission vs NDC

  • Planning Commission → Plan formulation, technical planning and evaluation.
  • NDC → Broader political and federal forum for development discussion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission → Technical Planning

NDC → Union-State Political Forum

32. Planning Commission and NDC — Working Relationship

  • The Planning Commission prepared Plans and development proposals.
  • The NDC facilitated broader discussion, consultation and political coordination.

33. Central Plan Assistance to States

  • The Planning Commission played an important role in determining Plan assistance to States.
  • States relied partly on Union transfers for development expenditure.
  • Assistance could include grants and loans from the Union Government.

34. Planning Commission — Influence through Plan Assistance

  • Its role in Plan assistance gave the Commission substantial practical influence over State development priorities.

35. Gadgil Formula

  • The Gadgil Formula was used to guide distribution of central Plan assistance among States.
  • It aimed to make distribution more objective.
  • Population and other development-related indicators formed part of the criteria.
  • The formula was modified over time.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gadgil Formula → Central Plan Assistance to States

36. Finance Commission — Constitutional Position

  • The Finance Commission is a constitutional body.
  • It recommends important aspects of tax devolution and certain grants between the Union and the States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Finance Commission → Constitutional

37. Planning Commission vs Finance Commission

  • Finance Commission → Constitutional body.
  • Planning Commission → Non-constitutional and non-statutory body.
  • Finance Commission → Tax devolution and certain grants.
  • Planning Commission → Historically involved in Plan assistance and development allocations.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Finance Commission ≠ Planning Commission

38. Centre-State Transfers — Two Historical Channels

During the planning era, Centre-State transfers broadly operated through:

  • Constitutional fiscal transfers involving the Finance Commission.
  • Planning-related transfers involving the Planning Commission.

39. Planning Commission — Poverty Reduction Role

  • Poverty reduction became increasingly important in later Five-Year Plans.
  • This was especially visible from the Fifth Plan onward.
  • Planning increasingly moved beyond output growth towards welfare and human development.

40. Planning Commission — Rural Employment and Food Security

  • Rural employment programmes became part of the development-planning framework.
  • Food security remained a major planning concern.
  • Agriculture, rural credit and rural infrastructure were linked with broader anti-poverty strategies.

41. Planning Commission — Social-Sector Role

Planning increasingly included:

  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Housing.
  • Drinking water.
  • Rural infrastructure.
  • Social protection.
  • Nutrition.
  • Skills.
📌 Must-Memorise

Later Planning → Growth + Human Development

42. Planning Commission — Poverty Estimation

  • The Planning Commission played an important role in official poverty estimation and poverty analysis.
  • Expert groups were appointed to review measurement methods.

43. Poverty Committees — Key Pairings

  • Lakdawala Committee → Poverty estimation.
  • Tendulkar Committee → Poverty estimation methodology.
  • Rangarajan Committee → Review of poverty measurement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tendulkar → Poverty Estimation

Rangarajan → Poverty Measurement Review

44. Planning Commission — Infrastructure Coordination

The Commission coordinated long-term investment in:

  • Electricity.
  • Roads.
  • Railways.
  • Ports.
  • Irrigation.
  • Telecommunications.
  • Urban infrastructure.

45. Planning Commission — Agriculture, Industry and Social Sector

Agriculture:

  • Irrigation.
  • Agricultural research.
  • Rural credit.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Productivity improvement.

Industry:

  • Heavy industry.
  • Public-sector enterprises.
  • Industrial infrastructure.

Social sector:

  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Nutrition.
  • Skills.
  • Social inclusion.

46. Sectoral Working Groups

  • Sectoral working groups and expert committees prepared recommendations in different areas of development.
  • These helped bring specialised knowledge into the planning process.

47. Planning Commission — Major Achievements

Important achievements included:

  • Systematic national planning.
  • Coordination across sectors.
  • Development of industrial capacity.
  • Expansion of irrigation.
  • Expansion of power generation.
  • Transport development.
  • Greater food self-sufficiency.
  • Expansion of education.
  • Expansion of health services.
  • Rural-development programmes.
  • Poverty-reduction programmes.
  • Medium-term development planning.
  • Long-term policy thinking.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission → Systematic National Development Framework

48. Planning Commission — Economic Data and Evaluation

  • The planning system encouraged greater use of economic data, quantitative targets and programme evaluation in public policy.
  • It helped bring separate government programmes into a more coordinated national framework.

49. Planning Commission — Excessive Centralisation Criticism

  • One of the major criticisms was excessive centralisation.
  • States argued that centrally determined priorities did not always reflect local conditions.
  • The Commission exercised considerable influence over States despite having no constitutional status.
📌 Must-Memorise

Major Criticism → Excessive Centralisation

50. Planning Commission — Fiscal and Federal Criticism

  • Its role in allocating Plan resources gave it substantial influence over State development.
  • The coexistence of Planning Commission and Finance Commission transfers complicated Centre-State fiscal relations.
  • Separate Plan and Non-Plan arrangements added further complexity.

51. Planning Commission — Top-Down Planning Criticism

  • The Commission was criticised for a top-down planning approach.
  • State and local priorities did not always receive sufficient flexibility.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission Criticism → Top-Down Planning

52. Local Participation — Major Limitation

  • Local Governments often had limited influence over major national planning decisions.
  • Community participation in priority setting was also considered inadequate.

53. Planning Commission — Implementation Problems

Major implementation problems included:

  • Delays.
  • Cost overruns.
  • Weak monitoring.
  • Coordination failures.
  • Administrative inefficiency.
  • Unrealistic targets.

54. Planning Commission — Implementation Limitation

  • The Commission formulated, coordinated and reviewed Plans.
  • Actual implementation depended heavily on Union Ministries, State Governments and local administrative systems.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Planning Commission → Formulation + Coordination

Not Sole Implementing Agency

55. Input-Oriented Planning Criticism

  • The planning system was often criticised for focusing heavily on how much money was allocated rather than on actual outcomes achieved.
  • This increased demand for outcome-based monitoring.
📌 Must-Memorise

Input-Oriented Planning → Allocation Focus

Outcome-Oriented Planning → Results Focus

56. One-Size-Fits-All Criticism

  • A highly centralised planning model could not always reflect India's diverse regional conditions.

States differ substantially in:

  • Income.
  • Population.
  • Geography.
  • Agriculture.
  • Industrialisation.
  • Human development.
  • Administrative capacity.

57. State-Specific Planning Need

  • Differences among States created demand for greater flexibility and State-specific development strategies.

58. Economic Reforms — 1991 and Planning

  • Economic reforms initiated in 1991 significantly changed India's economic environment.
  • The importance of centralised administrative control over production gradually declined.

59. Post-1991 Economic Changes

After reforms:

  • Industrial licensing reduced.
  • Private investment increased.
  • International trade expanded.
  • Foreign investment increased.
  • Market forces played a larger role in resource allocation.

60. Growing Economic Role of States

  • State Governments became increasingly important in attracting investment.
  • States developed their own industrial, infrastructure and development strategies.
  • Competition among States increased.

61. Directive to Indicative Planning Shift

  • Early planning involved stronger Government direction over production and investment.
  • After liberalisation, planning became increasingly indicative.
📌 Must-Memorise

Post-1991 → Directive Planning ↓ → Indicative Planning ↑

62. Indicative Planning — Meaning

Indicative planning focuses more on:

  • Strategic guidance.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Coordination.
  • Social development.
  • Policy support.
  • It involves less direct control over individual production decisions.

63. Competition Among States

Economic reforms increased competition among States for:

  • Investment.
  • Industry.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Employment.
  • Technology.

64. Cooperative Federalism — Growing Demand

  • Greater State participation increased demand for a more cooperative federal approach to development planning.

65. NITI Aayog — Establishment

  • The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015.
  • NITI Aayog was established on 1 January 2015.
📌 Must-Memorise

NITI Aayog → 1 January 2015

66. NITI Aayog — Full Form

NITI stands for:

National Institution for Transforming India

📌 Must-Memorise

NITI → National Institution for Transforming India

67. Why Planning Commission Was Replaced

Important reasons included:

  • Need for greater State participation.
  • Need for cooperative federalism.
  • Reduced relevance of centralised resource allocation.
  • Greater role of private investment.
  • Need for flexible policy design.
  • Greater emphasis on outcomes.
  • Greater emphasis on innovation.
  • Need for strategic long-term policy advice.

68. Planning Commission vs NITI Aayog

Planning Commission:

  • Centralised planning orientation.
  • Closely associated with Five-Year Plans.
  • Important role in Plan resource allocation.

NITI Aayog:

  • Cooperative federalism orientation.
  • Strategic policy advice.
  • Think-tank role.
  • Greater emphasis on flexibility and outcomes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission → Centralised Allocation

NITI Aayog → Cooperative Federalism + Policy Think Tank

69. Institutional Transition — Core Shift

The broad transition was:

Centralised Resource Allocation

→ Cooperative Federalism

→ Strategic Policy Coordination

→ Outcome Orientation

70. Twelfth Five-Year Plan — Final Plan

  • The Twelfth Five-Year Plan covered 2012–2017.
  • It became India's final Five-Year Plan.
  • India did not introduce a Thirteenth Five-Year Plan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Last Five-Year Plan → Twelfth Plan → 2012–2017

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

13th Five-Year Plan → Not Introduced

71. Abolition Did Not End Development Planning

  • Replacement of the Planning Commission did not mean development planning ended.
  • The institutional method changed from Five-Year Plan-based central allocation towards strategic policy coordination.

72. Planning System After 2015

The newer framework emphasised:

  • Strategic policymaking.
  • Cooperative federalism.
  • Greater State participation.
  • Outcome orientation.
  • Flexibility.
  • Policy coordination.

73. Planning Commission — Core Institutional Identity

Planning Commission =

1950

  • Executive Resolution
  • Non-Constitutional
  • Non-Statutory
  • Five-Year Plans
  • Resource Allocation
📌 Must-Memorise

This is the core institutional identity.

74. Planning Commission — Leadership Memory Chain

  • Chairman → Prime Minister.
  • Day-to-day leadership → Deputy Chairman.
  • Deputy Chairman → Cabinet Minister status.

75. Planning Commission — Function Memory Chain

  • Assess resources.
  • Identify shortages.
  • Set priorities.
  • Formulate Plans.
  • Allocate resources.
  • Review implementation.
  • Evaluate progress.
  • Recommend policy changes.

76. Planning Commission — Federal Memory Chain

  • State Plan discussions.
  • State development priorities.
  • Resource requirements.
  • Plan assistance.
  • Centre-State coordination.

77. Institutional Pairings

  • Planning Commission → Plan formulation + development allocation.
  • NDC → Union-State development forum.
  • Finance Commission → Constitutional fiscal transfers.
  • NITI Aayog → Strategic policy think tank.

78. Poverty Committee Pairings

  • Lakdawala → Poverty estimation.
  • Tendulkar → Poverty estimation methodology.
  • Rangarajan → Poverty measurement review.

79. Major Achievements — Memory Chain

  • Systematic national planning.
  • Industrial base.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Irrigation.
  • Power generation.
  • Food self-sufficiency.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Poverty reduction.
  • Long-term development planning.
  • Economic data and evaluation.

80. Major Criticisms — Memory Chain

  • Excessive centralisation.
  • Top-down planning.
  • Strong influence without constitutional status.
  • Overlap with Finance Commission.
  • Weak State flexibility.
  • Limited local participation.
  • Delays.
  • Cost overruns.
  • Weak monitoring.
  • Administrative inefficiency.
  • Unrealistic targets.
  • Input-oriented planning.

81. High-Yield Chronology

  • 15 March 1950 → Planning Commission established.
  • 1951 → First Five-Year Plan began.
  • 1952 → National Development Council established.
  • 1991 → Economic reforms began.
  • 1 January 2015 → NITI Aayog established.
  • 2015 → Planning Commission replaced.
  • 2012–2017 → Twelfth and final Five-Year Plan.
  • 2017 → Five-Year Plan era ended.

82. TNPSC Traps

  • Planning Commission was established in 1950, not 1951.
  • Exact establishment date → 15 March 1950.
  • Planning Commission was created by executive resolution.
  • It was not created by the Constitution.
  • It was not established by an Act of Parliament.
  • It was both non-constitutional and non-statutory.
  • Prime Minister was its Chairman.
  • Deputy Chairman handled much of the day-to-day functioning.
  • Deputy Chairman generally had Cabinet Minister status.
  • Planning Commission formulated Five-Year Plans.
  • It assessed resources and recommended resource allocation.
  • It was not the sole implementing agency.
  • NDC was established in 1952.
  • Prime Minister chaired the NDC.
  • Chief Ministers participated in the NDC.
  • Planning Commission and NDC were different institutions.
  • Gadgil Formula related to central Plan assistance to States.
  • Finance Commission is constitutional.
  • Planning Commission was non-constitutional.
  • Plan/Non-Plan expenditure is a historical classification.
  • Tendulkar Committee is associated with poverty estimation.
  • Rangarajan Committee reviewed poverty measurement.
  • Excessive centralisation was a major criticism.
  • Top-down planning was another major criticism.
  • Post-1991 planning became increasingly indicative.
  • NITI Aayog was established on 1 January 2015.
  • NITI stands for National Institution for Transforming India.
  • NITI Aayog emphasises cooperative federalism.
  • Planning Commission had an important resource-allocation role.
  • NITI Aayog primarily functions as a policy think tank.
  • Abolition of the Planning Commission did not end development policymaking.
  • Twelfth Plan was the last Five-Year Plan.
  • India did not introduce a Thirteenth Five-Year Plan.

83. Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • Planning Commission → 15 March 1950.
  • Status → Executive + Non-Constitutional + Non-Statutory.
  • Chairman → Prime Minister.
  • Deputy Chairman → Day-to-Day.
  • NDC → 1952.
  • Gadgil Formula → Plan Assistance.
  • Finance Commission → Constitutional.
  • Planning Commission → Non-Constitutional.
  • Tendulkar → Poverty.
  • Rangarajan → Poverty Review.
  • 1991 → Indicative Planning Shift.
  • NITI → 1 January 2015.
  • NITI → National Institution for Transforming India.
  • Planning Commission → Centralised.
  • NITI Aayog → Cooperative Federalism.
  • Twelfth Plan → 2012–2017.
  • Thirteenth Plan → None.

84. Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

  • Planning Commission established on? → 15 March 1950.
  • Created by? → Government of India executive resolution.
  • Constitutional body? → No.
  • Statutory body? → No.
  • Chairman? → Prime Minister.
  • Day-to-day functioning handled by? → Deputy Chairman.
  • Deputy Chairman generally had what status? → Cabinet Minister status.
  • Main role? → National development planning and Five-Year Plan formulation.
  • Did it assess resources? → Yes.
  • Did it set priorities? → Yes.
  • Did it recommend resource allocation? → Yes.
  • Did it review Plan progress? → Yes.
  • Was it the sole implementing agency? → No.
  • First Five-Year Plan began? → 1951.
  • NDC established? → 1952.
  • Chairman of NDC? → Prime Minister.
  • State representatives in NDC? → Chief Ministers.
  • Planning Commission vs NDC? → Technical planning vs broader Union-State forum.
  • Gadgil Formula related to? → Central Plan assistance to States.
  • Finance Commission status? → Constitutional.
  • Planning Commission status? → Non-constitutional.
  • Finance Commission mainly deals with? → Tax devolution and certain grants.
  • Planning Commission historically dealt with? → Plan assistance and development allocation.
  • Plan/Non-Plan expenditure classification current? → No; historical.
  • Planning Commission role in poverty? → Poverty estimation and analysis.
  • Tendulkar Committee? → Poverty estimation methodology.
  • Rangarajan Committee? → Poverty measurement review.
  • Major achievement? → Coordinated national development planning.
  • Major agricultural contribution? → Irrigation and food self-sufficiency.
  • Major industrial contribution? → Heavy industry and infrastructure.
  • Major criticism? → Excessive centralisation.
  • Another criticism? → Top-down approach.
  • Why was its status criticised? → It exercised substantial influence despite being non-constitutional.
  • Main implementation problems? → Delays, cost overruns, weak monitoring and coordination.
  • Input-oriented planning means? → Focus on allocation rather than outcomes.
  • What changed after 1991? → Markets and private investment became more important.
  • Planning shifted towards? → Indicative planning.
  • NITI Aayog established? → 1 January 2015.
  • Full form of NITI? → National Institution for Transforming India.
  • Planning Commission replaced in? → 2015.
  • Main federal idea associated with NITI Aayog? → Cooperative federalism.
  • Planning Commission orientation? → Centralised planning and resource allocation.
  • NITI Aayog orientation? → Strategic policy advice and cooperative federalism.
  • Last Five-Year Plan? → Twelfth Plan.
  • Twelfth Plan period? → 2012–2017.
  • Thirteenth Five-Year Plan introduced? → No.
  • Did abolition end development planning? → No; the institutional method changed.
